events.title: Rhetorica ad Herennium
events.text: The anonymous Roman handbook lists dozens of figures — the catalogue becomes a teachable system alongside Aristotle's.

events.title: Swift, A Modest Proposal
events.text: Irony carries a moral argument so fierce that plain statement would have failed.

events.title: Churchill's anaphora
events.text: "We shall fight on the beaches… we shall fight in the fields" — repetition widens the terrain into a drumbeat of refusal.

events.title: Empson, Seven Types of Ambiguity
events.text: The best figures hold several meanings at once — and mean them all.

events.title: Lakoff & Johnson, Metaphors We Live By
events.text: Metaphor is the structure of ordinary thought, not decoration — the catalogue becomes a citizenship skill.

activities.caption: file each figure by its mechanism
activities.name: fosMechanismBuckets

config.prompt: Tropes move meaning, schemes arrange structure — file each figure:

items.label: metonymy — the associate stands for the thing
personification — human agency to the non-human
parallelism — matched clauses in a row

config.why: Tropes work on content, schemes on structure — and the great persuasive passages usually combine both.

activities.anchor: the poem works by transferring bird-properties
activities.caption: pair each figure with its tenor-and-vehicle analysis
activities.name: fosTenorMatch

config.prompt: Analyse the transfer — pair each figure with its tenor, vehicle and posture:

pairs.right: tenor: hope · vehicle: a bird — perching, singing wordless songs, enduring a gale transferred onto the feeling

pairs.left: "my love is like a red, red rose"
pairs.right: a simile — same transfer, connective kept visible, which can be gentler or more wry
personification — mortality becomes a courteous suitor, terror converted into courtliness

pairs.left: "she left in tears and a taxi"
pairs.right: zeugma — one verb yokes the emotional and the mundane into the same event

config.why: Naming tenor and vehicle is only half the analysis — the earnable sentence states what the transfer imports.

activities.anchor: These two are the most confused pair
activities.caption: walk the part-or-associate test
activities.name: fosTestBranch

config.root: Walk the part-or-associate test — the diagnostic that separates synecdoche from metonymy.

start.text: Figure 1: "boots on the ground". The substitute is boots. Is a boot a part or member of a soldier, or merely connected with the soldier?

choices.label: Part or member — the boot stands for the soldier it belongs to
Merely connected — boots are kit you associate with soldiers

boots-part.text: Synecdoche: the lesson files "boots on the ground" as part-for-whole — it counts soldiers the way "all hands on deck" counts sailors by their working hands and "nice wheels" praises a car by its tyres.

choices.label: Test the next figure: "the Crown decided"

boots-associate.text: The lesson rules this synecdoche, not metonymy: "boots on the ground" counts soldiers part-for-whole — re-run the test before the second figure.

choices.label: Re-run the test, then continue to "the Crown decided"

crown.text: Figure 2: "the Crown decided". Is a crown a part or member of the monarch, or merely connected with the monarch?

choices.label: Part or member — a crown is the monarch's own head-gear
Merely connected — regalia stand beside the throne

crown-part.text: Careful — this is the trap the test exists to catch: a crown is not a part or member of the monarch, it is regalia connected with the throne. The lesson files "the Crown decided" as metonymy — the associate, not a part.

crown-associate.text: Metonymy: the substitute is a closely associated thing — the Crown for the monarch or government, the pen for writing, the whole town for its people.

config.why: Part or member → synecdoche; merely connected → metonymy. And the stakes are political: calling workers "hands" makes labour a commodity you can hire by the dozen.

activities.caption: find the line the definition refutes
activities.name: fosIronySpot

config.prompt: One line of this irony report is wrong — click it:
lines: Swift calmly proposing to solve Irish poverty by eating babies (1729) is irony carrying a moral argument.
Dramatic irony is the stage version — the audience knows what the speaker does not.
Duncan's "this castle hath a pleasant seat" is dramatic irony: we know what awaits him.
Verbal irony always requires a sarcastic tone of voice to land.
Dramatic irony makes the reader complicit with the author rather than the character.
config.correction: No tone of voice required — verbal irony is a gap the reader is invited to see over the speaker's head; sarcasm is only its sharpest spoken form.
config.why: The gap, not the tone of voice, is the definition — and dramatic irony needs no speaker intending anything at all.

activities.caption: drag the divider — the frame before and after naming
activities.name: fosFrameCompare

config.prompt: Political language is a war of frames — drag the divider to name the figure:

before.label: The phrase as spun
before.text: "Tax relief" — the affliction frame presupposed: tax as a disease, relief as cure, the virtue quietly allocated before any argument begins. One law, two metaphors, different poll numbers.

after.label: The figure named
after.text: Once you can say "that is a metonymy hiding people inside logistics" or "that is a metaphor casting tax as affliction", the phrase loses its anaesthetic — the same reflex the statistics ladder builds for numbers, applied to words.

config.why: Metaphor runs ordinary thought — which is why recognising a frame is a citizenship skill, not an English-room exercise.

activities.anchor: Two sentences, one of them doing all the work
activities.caption: rebuild the essay check, step by step
activities.name: fosEssayOrder

config.prompt: Rebuild the revision check the lesson prescribes for every named figure:
items: Name the figure in the draft.
State its job — what does it accomplish that plain statement could not?
If a paraphrase without the figure loses nothing, it was decoration and the analysis is empty.
If it loses something, you have found the sentence the examiner is waiting for.
config.why: A spotter's list earns nothing — the marks come from the second sentence, which states the figure's job.

activities.anchor: One more device is worth naming because it is everywhere and often missed
activities.caption: fill the missing word in the definition
activities.name: fosAllusionCloze

config.text: Allusion is quotation made %%0%%: it imports a whole earlier text as its setting — Eliot's "April is the cruellest month" means both Aprils at once, Chaucer's included.
config.hint: The lesson's own compound — what walls carry, and what borrowed references do.
